key_terms.meaning: Track a marked fluid particle through space and time; its position is r(t).
Describe the velocity field V(x, y, z, t) at fixed points in space.
A fixed mass of fluid, also called a closed system; no mass crosses its boundary.
A fixed region in space through which fluid may flow; mass, momentum, and energy cross its boundary.
Velocity at any fixed point does not change with time: ∂V/∂t = 0.
Fluid moves in smooth, orderly layers with no macroscopic mixing.
Fluid motion is chaotic with random eddies and fluctuations.
A curve whose tangent at every point is along the instantaneous velocity vector.
The actual trajectory traced by a single fluid particle over time.
The locus of all particles that have passed through a given fixed point.
The part ∂V/∂t of a particle's acceleration due to change of velocity with time at a fixed point.
The part (V·∇)V of acceleration due to the particle moving to a place with different velocity.
Conservation of mass: ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·(ρV) = 0.
Twice the angular velocity of a fluid element: ζ = ∇ × V.
Flow in which the vorticity is zero everywhere: ∇ × V = 0.
For 2-D incompressible flow, u = ∂ψ/∂y and v = −∂ψ/∂x; ψ is constant along a streamline.
For irrotational flow, V = ∇φ; φ exists only when vorticity is zero.
A grid of streamlines and equipotential lines drawn to solve 2-D potential flow graphically.
A swirling flow with vθ = K/r and zero vorticity except at the centre.
A swirling flow with vθ = ωr, like a rigid body, with uniform vorticity.

takeaways: The Eulerian view describes the velocity field at fixed points; the Lagrangian view follows individual particles; both give the same physics.
A system is a fixed mass; a control volume is a fixed region in space; the Reynolds transport theorem connects them.
Steady means no change with time at a point; uniform means no change with place at an instant.
Streamlines, pathlines, and streaklines are different curves; they coincide only in steady flow.
A fluid particle's acceleration has a local part ∂V/∂t and a convective part (V·∇)V.
The continuity equation expresses conservation of mass for a control volume.
Vorticity ∇×V measures the spin of a fluid element; curved streamlines can still be irrotational.
The stream function exists for any 2-D incompressible flow; the velocity potential exists only for irrotational flow.
A flow net gives velocity from the spacing of streamlines and discharge from the number of flow channels.
A free vortex has vθ = K/r and zero vorticity away from the centre; a forced vortex has vθ = ωr and uniform vorticity.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for derivations of acceleration and continuity, clear distinctions among flow lines and flow types, and worked problems on stream function, vorticity, flow nets, and free or forced vortices.

bank.q: Define a system and a control volume. Explain the Lagrangian and Eulerian approaches to describing fluid motion, with one example of each.
outline: Control volume: fixed region, mass crosses boundary
Lagrangian: follow a marked particle, r(t)
Eulerian: field V(x, y, z, t) at fixed points
Examples: dye patch vs. velocity probe

bank.q: Classify fluid flows as steady or unsteady, uniform or non-uniform, laminar or turbulent, and rotational or irrotational. Give one practical example of each pair.
outline: Uniform: same velocity everywhere; non-uniform: varies with place
Laminar: orderly layers; turbulent: chaotic eddies
Examples: pipe flow, river flood, honey vs. fast water, free vs. forced vortex

bank.q: Explain streamlines, pathlines, and streaklines. State the condition under which they coincide, and define a stream tube.
outline: Streamline: tangent to velocity at an instant
Streakline: locus of particles passing a fixed point
Stream tube: bundle of streamlines, no flow across walls

bank.q: Define vorticity and circulation. Show that a flow can be irrotational even when streamlines are curved.
outline: Curved streamlines do not imply rotation; example: free vortex away from centre

bank.q: Define the stream function and the velocity potential. State the conditions under which each exists and give the velocity components in terms of each.
outline: Stream function ψ: exists for 2-D incompressible flow
Velocity potential φ: exists for irrotational flow

bank.q: A velocity field is given by V = (3x)i + (−2y)j m/s. Find the acceleration of a fluid particle at the point (1, 2) m.
For a two-dimensional incompressible flow, u = 2x and v = −2y. Check continuity and find the stream function.
Water flows through a pipe that narrows from 0.2 m diameter to 0.1 m diameter. If the velocity in the wider section is 1.5 m/s, find the velocity in the narrower section.
A free vortex has tangential velocity vθ = 5/r m/s. Find the vorticity at r = 2 m and at r = 0.5 m.
outline: Vorticity is zero everywhere except r = 0

bank.q: Draw a flow net for flow between two parallel plates and explain how it gives the velocity and discharge.
outline: Discharge per unit depth: q = Δψ per channel
Total Q = number of channels × Δψ

bank.q: Compare free and forced vortex flow. Derive the pressure variation and the shape of the free surface for each.
outline: Free vortex: vθ = K/r, irrotational away from centre
Forced vortex: p = p₀ + ½ρω²r²; free surface is a paraboloid

bank.q: Derive the three-dimensional continuity equation for a control volume and reduce it to the steady incompressible two-dimensional form.
outline: Mass balance: rate of mass out − in = −∂m_cv/∂t

bank.q: A velocity field is given by u = 4x, v = −4y. Determine whether the flow is irrotational. If so, find the velocity potential and the stream function.
outline: Velocity potential: u = ∂φ/∂x → φ = 2x² + f(y); v = ∂φ/∂y → f'(y) = −4y → φ = 2x² − 2y²
Stream function: u = ∂ψ/∂y → ψ = 4xy + g(x); v = −∂ψ/∂x → g'(x) = 0 → ψ = 4xy
Check: φ and ψ satisfy Laplace equation

bank.q: Explain the physical meaning of local and convective acceleration. Use the examples of flow in a nozzle and flow in a pipe bend to discuss when each term is important.
outline: Local: ∂V/∂t, important in unsteady flow (starting pump)
Convective: (V·∇)V, important when velocity changes along path
Nozzle: steady flow, convective acceleration dominates
Pipe bend: direction changes, convective acceleration normal to flow

glossary.def: A very small mass of fluid that moves as a single unit.
The rate of change following a fluid particle: D/Dt = ∂/∂t + V·∇.
The rate of change at a fixed point: ∂/∂t.
The change due to motion through a spatial gradient: (V·∇).
Flow in which velocity at a fixed point does not change with time.
Flow in which velocity at a fixed point changes with time.
Flow in which velocity is the same everywhere at a given instant.
Flow in which velocity varies from point to point.
Smooth, layered flow with no macroscopic mixing.
Chaotic flow with random eddies and fluctuations.
A curve everywhere tangent to the instantaneous velocity.
The trajectory of a single fluid particle.
The locus of particles that have passed through a fixed point.
A tube formed by streamlines; no flow crosses its walls.
The curl of velocity, ∇×V; twice the angular velocity of a fluid element.
The line integral of velocity around a closed curve: Γ = ∮V·dl.
Flow with zero vorticity everywhere.
A scalar ψ with u = ∂ψ/∂y, v = −∂ψ/∂x for 2-D incompressible flow.
A scalar φ with V = ∇φ for irrotational flow.
A line on which the velocity potential is constant.
A mesh of streamlines and equipotential lines.
An irrotational, incompressible flow that can be described by a velocity potential.
A vortex with vθ = K/r and zero vorticity away from the axis.
A vortex with vθ = ωr and uniform vorticity, like a rotating rigid body.
Flow in which velocity depends on two space coordinates and time.
A fixed region in space used for mass and momentum balances.
